title: Jay M. Fonticella
text: Greetings! My name is Jay Fonticella, and I am a second-year Systems Biology and Bioinformatics PhD student at Case Western. As an undergraduate at Tufts University, I explored the morphological pathways underlying craniofacial tissue repair in Xenopus laevis (African clawed frog), delineating how the peripheral nervous system contributes to craniofacial cartilage and muscle repair (doi: 10.3390/jdb13030026). As a post-baccalaureate at the Harvard Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, I investigated how metabolism underlies cancer cell biology and chemoresistance, demonstrating a novel mechanism whereby redox biology underpinned chemotherapy drug tolerance in ovarian cancer models (doi: 10.1038/s41586-025-08756-y).

title: Jay M. Fonticella
text:
About Me
Now, I am a graduate student in the Stamler laboratory based at the UH Harrington Discovery Institute and CWRU Institute for Transformative Molecular Medicine, wherein we study the functional consequences of S-nitrosylation (i.e., the reactive nitrogen species side of redox biology) on cell signaling and physiological functions.
My project currently focuses on delineating how S-nitrosoglutathione — one of the many macromolecules in our cells that can carry a nitric oxide (NO) functional group — is recognized in tissues and cells. By elucidating novel recognition mechanisms, my work aims to contribute to the growing literature on enzymatic mechanisms by which this post-translational modification pathway defined as S-nitrosylation can come about. To rigorously pioneer this line of work, I am collating machine learning, biophysics, genetics, and biochemistry approaches. Thank you so much for visiting, and please feel free to send me a message to learn more!

Download my CV (PDF)

Pictured: a ball-and-stick model of S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO), the molecule my thesis work centers on.

title: Welcome to My Blog
text:
Welcome! This blog is where I will share updates on my research in redox and nitrosative biology, notes on the computational and wet-lab methods in use, and the rollercoaster that’s bound to become the life of a PhD student at Case Western.
My front image depicts S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO), a small molecule in which glutathione carries a nitric oxide group on its cysteine sulfur (represented here as a yellow atom). As an open-ended area in the field, understanding how cells and tissues recognize GSNO is the focus of my thesis work, and I look forward to writing more about it here.
Thank you so much for reading, and feel free to connect by email.

title: Who Has High Blood Pressure? Age, BMI, Sex, and Race/Ethnicity in NHANES 2017–2020
text:
4.1 How I defined hypertension
My primary outcome follows the definition used in both NCHS reports [1, 2], which comes from the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline [3]: a participant has hypertension if their average systolic pressure is at least 130 mmHg, or their average diastolic pressure is at least 80 mmHg, or they report currently taking prescribed medicine for high blood pressure. Including medication matters: a person whose blood pressure is well controlled by treatment still has hypertension.
I was careful not to over-read what this variable measures. NHANES measures blood pressure at a single visit, while a clinical diagnosis requires elevated readings on at least two separate occasions. My outcome is therefore a survey classification of hypertension, which is what national surveillance reports use, rather than a clinical diagnosis. Because the 130/80 threshold is newer and lower than the older 140/90 threshold from the JNC 7 report, I also repeated the main analyses with the 140/90 definition to see whether any conclusion depended on that choice.

8.1 Who was in the sample?


Show the R code
summarise_group <- function(data) {
  tibble(
    `Participants, n`       = fmt_int(nrow(data)),
    `Age, mean (SD), years` = paste0(fmt_num(mean(data$age)), " (",
                                     fmt_num(sd(data$age)), ")"),
    `BMI, mean (SD), kg/m²` = paste0(fmt_num(mean(data$bmi)), " (",
                                     fmt_num(sd(data$bmi)), ")"),

    `Taking BP medicine, %` = fmt_pct(mean(data$bp_med == 1)),
    `Mean SBP / DBP, mmHg`  = paste0(fmt_num(mean(data$sbp_mean), 0), " / ",

The sample includes 7,019 adults with a mean age of 49.4 years and a mean BMI of 30.2 kg/m². Overall, 54.6% (90% CI 53.6% to 55.6%) met the 130/80 definition of hypertension, and 28.8% reported taking blood-pressure medicine. Under the older 140/90 definition, prevalence was 39.6%. These are percentages of this unweighted sample, so they should not be compared directly with the survey-weighted national estimates in the NCHS reports.

title: Who Has High Blood Pressure? Age, BMI, Sex, and Race/Ethnicity in NHANES 2017–2020
text:
8.2 H1: Age


Show the R code
plot_prevalence(prev_age, "age_group", "Age group (years)")








Figure 2: Hypertension prevalence by age group, with 90% Wilson confidence intervals.





Prevalence rose from 26.4% among adults aged 21–39 to 57.7% among those aged 40–59 and 77.9% among those aged 60–79 (Cochran–Armitage trend test p < 0.001). After adjusting for BMI, sex, and race/ethnicity, each additional 10 years of age was associated with 1.94 times the odds (90% CI 1.88 to 2.01), i.e., 94% higher odds. H1 was supported.

title: Who Has High Blood Pressure? Age, BMI, Sex, and Race/Ethnicity in NHANES 2017–2020
text:
8.3 H2: Body mass index

Show the R code
plot_bmi_histogram(htn_data)
plot_bmi_by_htn(htn_data)












(a) Distribution of BMI











(b) BMI by hypertension status







Figure 3: Distribution of BMI and BMI by hypertension status. Dashed lines in (a) mark the CDC category cut-points.





Show the R code
plot_prevalence(prev_bmi, "bmi_cat", "BMI category (kg/m²)") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) str_replace(x, " \\(", "\n("))








Figure 4: Hypertension prevalence by BMI category, with 90% Wilson confidence intervals.





BMI is right-skewed, with a long tail of high values. Adults classified as having hypertension had a mean BMI 2.9 kg/m² higher than adults without it (90% CI 2.6 to 3.2; Welch t-test p < 0.001), and the medians differed in the same direction (30.3 vs. 27.4 kg/m²). Prevalence rose from 39.8% at a healthy weight to 67.9% among adults with class 2–3 obesity (trend test p < 0.001). In the adjusted model, each additional 5 kg/m² of BMI was associated with 1.39 times the odds (90% CI 1.34 to 1.44), i.e., 39% higher odds. H2 was supported.

title: Who Has High Blood Pressure? Age, BMI, Sex, and Race/Ethnicity in NHANES 2017–2020
text:
8.4 H3: Biological sex


Show the R code
plot_prevalence(prev_sex, "sex", "Sex")








Figure 5: Hypertension prevalence by sex, with 90% Wilson confidence intervals.





Hypertension prevalence was 58.3% in men and 51.0% in women, a difference of 7.2 percentage points (90% CI 5.3 to 9.2; p < 0.001). After adjustment, men had 1.51 times the odds (90% CI 1.38 to 1.65), i.e., 51% higher odds compared with women. H3 was supported.

title: Who Has High Blood Pressure? Age, BMI, Sex, and Race/Ethnicity in NHANES 2017–2020
text:
8.5 H4: Race/ethnicity


Show the R code
plot_prevalence(prev_race, "race_eth", NULL, horizontal = TRUE)








Figure 6: Hypertension prevalence by race/ethnicity (unadjusted), with 90% Wilson confidence intervals.





Unadjusted prevalence ranged from 43.8% among Mexican American adults to 65.5% among Non-Hispanic Black adults (chi-square test p < 0.001). After adjustment for age, BMI, and sex, the overall likelihood-ratio test for race/ethnicity gave p < 0.001. Compared with Non-Hispanic White adults, the adjusted odds were clearly higher for Non-Hispanic Black, Non-Hispanic Asian and Other/Multiracial and clearly lower for Mexican American; the interval included 1 for Other Hispanic. H4 was supported.

Show the R code
plot_forest(res$or_compare)








Figure 7: Adjusted odds ratios from the primary model (blue) and the 140/90 sensitivity model (orange). The dashed line marks an odds ratio of 1 (no association).







Show the R code
plot_predictions(res$predictions)








Figure 8: Model-predicted probability of hypertension by age and BMI, for Non-Hispanic White women and men (the reference race/ethnicity group). Shaded bands are 90% confidence intervals.





The adjusted model shows how the four factors work together. Comparing the unadjusted and adjusted columns of Table 4 shows how much each association changes once the other variables are held constant. Differences between the two columns are expected for race/ethnicity in particular, because the groups have different age and BMI distributions. The predicted-probability curves in Figure 8 translate the odds ratios back into probabilities, which are easier to interpret: the gap between BMI curves shows the BMI effect at every age.
The model separated people with and without hypertension reasonably well (C-statistic 0.789), and across ten deciles of predicted risk, observed and predicted prevalence differed by at most 3.0 percentage points.

title: Who Has High Blood Pressure? Age, BMI, Sex, and Race/Ethnicity in NHANES 2017–2020
text:
8.7 Sensitivity analysis
Some estimates change direction or significance under the stricter 140/90 mmHg threshold: Mexican American (vs. Non-Hispanic White) and Other Hispanic (vs. Non-Hispanic White). Those particular results depend on the definition used. Under the 140/90 definition, overall prevalence in the sample was 39.6% rather than 54.6%, as expected for a higher threshold.


Show the R code
res$hypotheses |>
  transmute(Hypothesis = hypothesis, Evidence = evidence, Verdict = verdict) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_body(columns = Verdict)) |>
  style_gt()




Table 5: Summary of the four hypotheses (decision rule: α = 0.10 and a 90% CI that excludes 1).









Hypothesis
Evidence
Verdict




H1: Older adults have a higher prevalence of hypertension.
Trend test p < 0.001; adjusted OR per 10 years 1.94 (1.88 to 2.01)
Supported


H2: Higher BMI is associated with a higher prevalence of hypertension.
Trend test p < 0.001; adjusted OR per 5 kg/m² 1.39 (1.34 to 1.44)
Supported


H3: Hypertension prevalence differs by biological sex.
Chi-square p < 0.001; adjusted OR (male vs. female) 1.51 (1.38 to 1.65)
Supported (higher odds in men)


H4: Hypertension prevalence differs across race/ethnicity groups.
Chi-square p < 0.001; adjusted likelihood-ratio test p < 0.001
Supported
